activities.caption: divide the budget by function — file each claim under its macro
activities.name: nutMacroSort

config.prompt: Three macronutrients, one budget — file each claim:

items.label: 9 kcal/g — abundant, and essential for hormone production
structural amino acids for repair and growth
stocks the glycogen tank sized at roughly 1,600–2,000 kcal
rarely below about 1 g/kg/day — chronic low intake degrades hormones
used appreciably as fuel only when carbohydrate runs short

config.why: Prescriptions arrive per kilogram, never as percentages: carbohydrate 3–5 g/kg on easy days rising to 5–10 for heavy endurance work, protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg for strength goals.

activities.anchor: carbohydrate strategy is periodised like training itself
activities.caption: the fuelling timeline of a long event — in order
activities.name: nutFuelOrder

config.prompt: An event beyond 90 minutes approaches — order the carbohydrate moves:
items: 2–3 days out: carbo-load at 8–12 g/kg/day while training tapers — glycogen stores rise 20–40%
2–4 hours before: a carbohydrate-focused meal tops the tank
During, beyond 90 minutes: exogenous carbohydrate at roughly 60–90 g/h, mixed glucose and fructose
After exhaustive work: about 1–1.2 g/kg/h in the hours when next-day training matters
config.why: The mixture absorbs faster than either sugar alone — glucose rides SGLT1, fructose rides GLUT5 — and spares liver glycogen.

activities.caption: size a meal above the trigger
activities.name: nutMealEst

config.prompt: Protein is distributed across meals of roughly 0.3–0.4 g/kg each. For a 70 kg athlete, how many grams per meal?
config.why: 0.3–0.4 × 70 ≈ 21–28 g — enough to clear the leucine threshold (about 2–3 g of leucine) that maximally stimulates synthesis per meal.
config.context: Total daily intake dominates; timing around training is a fine-tuning, not a cliff edge.

activities.anchor: Fluid balance is a performance variable
activities.caption: mark where endurance performance starts to slip
activities.name: nutDehydPlace

config.prompt: Place the dehydration level (as % of body mass) at which endurance performance measurably degrades:
config.why: About 2% of body mass — more in heat. Weigh before and after: each kilogram lost is roughly a litre of sweat to replace.

activities.anchor: Group A holds supplements with strong proof
activities.caption: the evidence tier — pair each supplement with its file
activities.name: nutSuppMatch

config.prompt: Match each supplement to what the evidence actually says:

pairs.right: 3–5 g/day tops up the phosphocreatine tank — the most-studied supplement in sports science
3–6 mg/kg about 60 minutes before — improves endurance and lowers perceived effort
moderate benefits for sub-elite endurance performance
3–6 g/day for weeks — buffering that helps events of roughly 1–4 minutes

config.why: Supplements are a topping — worth a percent or two only on top of fuelling, training and sleep done right; under strict liability, what is in the tub is the athlete's responsibility.

activities.anchor: the body budgets like a famine
activities.caption: call the energy-availability floor
activities.name: nutRedsEst

config.prompt: Energy availability is dietary energy minus exercise energy, per kg of fat-free mass. Below roughly what daily value (kcal/kg fat-free mass) does the RED-S cascade begin?
config.why: Below roughly 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass per day (the healthy floor is around 45), reproductive hormones shut down, bone formation stalls and immunity degrades.
config.context: Performance declines below the floor even as body mass falls — the runner gets slower and sicker.

activities.anchor: Prescriptions become real when they are priced onto an athlete
activities.caption: one line of this worked day is wrong — click it
activities.name: nutDaySpot

config.prompt: One line of these three worked days is mispriced — click it:
lines: The marathoner (70 kg): carbohydrate 6–8 g/kg = 420–560 g across the day.
Her protein: 1.4 g/kg ≈ 100 g, spread over four meals of 25 g.
The strength athlete (80 kg): protein at 2.0 g/kg = 130 g.
His carbohydrate around sessions: 4–6 g/kg = 320–480 g on training days.
The footballer on match day: in-match carbohydrate at ~30–60 g/h for the second half.
config.correction: 2.0 g/kg × 80 kg = 160 g — four feedings of 40 g, the growth lever the surplus equips.
config.why: The arithmetic is the prescription: carbohydrate scaled to the day's engine work, protein scaled to repair, fluid scaled to sweat.

activities.anchor: Three factors sit outside the macro tables
activities.caption: true or false — the quiet levers
activities.name: nutLeverJudge

statements.s: Restriction under about 7 hours of sleep measurably reduces glycogen resynthesis and raises injury rates.
statements.why: Sleep hygiene is nutrition policy by other means — regular times, dark cool rooms, caffeine cut-off eight hours before.

statements.s: A post-match pint helps the evening's recovery.
statements.why: After exercise alcohol impairs muscle-protein synthesis and rehydration — a diuretic that blunts the drive to refuel.

statements.s: Jet lag degrades performance for roughly one day per time zone crossed.
statements.why: Light-exposure timing helps; so does watching the appetite drift that quietly accumulates RED-S risk.

statements.s: Long-haul athletes tend to over-eat because travel disrupts routine.
statements.why: They under-eat precisely when energy needs are high — which is where the risk sits.
